answer:
The Phillips curve (PC) is the short-run empirical relationship showing a negative correlation between inflation $\\pi$ and unemployment $u$: when unemployment is lower, inflation tends to be higher (and vice versa).

A standard way to write it is:

$$
\\pi = \\pi^{e} - \\alpha (u - u^{n}) + \\nu
$$

Here $\\pi^{e}$ is expected inflation, $u^{n}$ is the natural rate of unemployment, $\\alpha>0$ measures how strongly inflation responds when $u$ moves away from $u^{n}$, and $\\nu$ is a “cost-push” (supply) shock term.

The key Friedman point from the course materials is that policymakers can’t pick a permanently “better” point (low $u$, high $\\pi$) on a fixed curve: if they keep trying to hold $u<u^{n}$, expectations adjust ($\\pi^{e}$ rises) and the PC shifts (so you end up with higher inflation without permanently lower unemployment).

Cournot vs Bertrand is mainly WHAT firms choose as their strategic variable.

Cournot competition: firms compete by choosing quantity $q_i$ (often simultaneously), then the market price comes from inverse demand $P(Q)$ where $Q=\sum_i q_i$.

Bertrand competition: firms compete by choosing price $p_i$ simultaneously for identical products; consumers buy from the lowest-price firm.

In the basic Bertrand model with identical products and no capacity constraints, the Nash equilibrium has firms pricing at marginal cost, $p=MC$, so profits are driven to zero; in Cournot, limiting quantity typically keeps price above marginal cost, $P>MC$, so profits can be positive.

Logistic regression in the notes is a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) for a binary outcome $Y \in \{0,1\}$, where you model a probability by taking the usual linear index and passing it through a nonlinear “link” function:

$$
\Pr(Y=1 \mid X)=F(\beta_0+\beta_1 X)
$$

Here $\beta_0+\beta_1X$ is the INDEX (same linear combination as in OLS), and $F(\cdot)$ is chosen so predictions stay between 0 and 1 (unlike OLS, which can predict outside that range). In logit, the link function is the logistic CDF:

$$
F(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}
$$

A common interpretation uses log-odds:

$$
\log\left(\frac{\Pr(Y=1\mid X)}{1-\Pr(Y=1\mid X)}\right)=\beta_0+\beta_1X
$$

So $\beta_1$ is the change in LOG-ODDS from a one-unit increase in $X$; the change in probability (the marginal effect) depends on where you are on the S-curve (i.e., on $X$ through $F(\beta_0+\beta_1X)$).

Bootstrap idea: approximate a sampling distribution by re-sampling from your ONE observed dataset (sampling WITH replacement) and recomputing the statistic many times.

Core procedure (as in the course materials):
1. Start with a dataset of $N$ observations.
2. Draw a “bootstrap sample” by sampling $N$ observations WITH replacement from the dataset.
3. Compute the statistic of interest on that bootstrap sample (mean, regression coefficient, etc.).
4. Repeat steps 2–3 many times (often a few thousand).
5. Use the empirical distribution of those replicated statistics to get a standard error, confidence interval, etc.

Key caveats highlighted: the plain bootstrap works best with decently large samples and well-behaved i.i.d. data; it can perform poorly with small samples, extreme skew, and dependence (like autocorrelation or certain panel structures) unless you use a modified bootstrap (e.g., cluster-aware approaches).

The course materials don’t use the term “comparative advantage” explicitly in the excerpts we have, but they make the core point behind it: autarky (each household making everything itself) is poor, and societies get richer when people specialize and trade.

They emphasize that “in the end, there’s only us, the people,” so the way to raise living standards is reorganizing who produces what through cooperation, firms, and markets, rather than everyone producing their own consumption. The Ford production-line example is a specialization story: the same workers and tools produced more by dividing tasks and specializing.

Comparative advantage is the formal version of that idea: specialize in what you can produce at lower opportunity cost, then trade. Opportunity cost is usually written as

$$OC_X = \frac{a_{LX}}{a_{LY}}$$

where $a_{LX}$ is labor needed per unit of $X$ (and similarly for $Y$). In that framework, trade is beneficial even if one person is “better” at producing everything in absolute terms, as long as opportunity costs differ.

Money multiplier = how many dollars of money supply $M$ the banking system can create from 1 extra dollar of “high-powered money” (reserves/monetary base) injected by the Fed (like in an open market purchase).

Core formula from our setup (when people hold no cash, so $CU=0$):

$$m = \frac{1}{RR}$$

where $RR$ is the reserve ratio (fraction of deposits banks keep as reserves). Then:

$$\Delta M = m \cdot \Delta \text{Reserves}$$

Intuition: when the Fed injects reserves, banks lend out the “excess” reserves; those loans get spent and redeposited in banks; banks keep fraction $RR$ and re-lend the rest; this repeats as a geometric series. A LOWER $RR$ makes the series larger, so the multiplier is bigger; a HIGHER $RR$ shrinks it.

If your notes also allow people to hold cash (a “currency drain”), the multiplier gets smaller because some money leaks out of deposits into cash, so less gets re-lent each round.
